questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with 15 skin lesions showing a mixture of well-defined plaques with some ill-defined papules. Histopathology reveals granulomas composed of immature epithelioid cells admixed with macrophages, and slit-skin smear shows a Bacteriological Index of 2+. Which position on the Ridley-Jopling spectrum best describes this patient's disease?
questions.exp: Mid-Borderline (BB) leprosy sits at the immunological midpoint of the spectrum, displaying true dimorphous features with a mixture of tuberculoid (immature epithelioid cells) and lepromatous (macrophages) characteristics. The BI of 2-3+ and 10-30 skin lesions are typical of BB leprosy.

questions.q: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with intense vulvar pruritus for 6 months. Examination reveals ivory-white atrophic plaques with a 'cigarette-paper' texture involving the vulva and perianal region in a figure-of-eight configuration. The vaginal mucosa appears normal. Which autoantibody is most likely to be detected in this patient?
questions.exp: This presentation is classic for vulvar Lichen Sclerosus et Atrophicus. Circulating IgG autoantibodies against Extracellular Matrix Protein 1 (ECM-1) are found in approximately 80% of patients with LS, making it a highly specific serological marker for this condition.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with widespread, asymmetric, irregular, branching violaceous discoloration on her trunk and extremities that persists despite warming. She also reports a history of recurrent miscarriages. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.exp: The patient has livedo racemosa (asymmetric, persistent, widespread) with recurrent pregnancy loss, which is characteristic of antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLS). Livedo racemosa is present in up to 70% of SLE-associated APLS and serves as a predictor for thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss.

questions.q: A patient with confirmed Sézary syndrome is being counseled about prognosis. The oncologist explains that the median overall survival is approximately 32-35 months. What is the most common cause of death in patients with Sézary syndrome?
opts: Visceral organ infiltration by tumor cells
questions.exp: In Sézary syndrome, the massive leukemic expansion of malignant T-cells eradicates normal immunity, and mortality is predominantly driven by opportunistic infections. Severe skin barrier disruption further compounds the immunocompromised state.

questions.q: Regarding the natural course of untreated Mid-Borderline (BB) leprosy, which of the following statements is most accurate?
opts: BB is immunologically stable and rarely transitions to other forms
Upgrading towards the tuberculoid pole is more common than downgrading
Downgrading towards the lepromatous pole is more common than upgrading
BB maintains a stable equilibrium between host immunity and bacillary load indefinitely
questions.exp: BB leprosy is the most immunologically unstable stage on the Ridley-Jopling spectrum. In the natural course without treatment, downgrading (shifting toward BL and LL) is far more common as the host's immune system gradually loses its ability to contain bacillary multiplication.

questions.q: A tissue biopsy from a mycetoma shows Gram-positive branching filaments measuring 0.8 μm in diameter. Modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain using 1% H₂SO₄ shows partial acid-fastness. Which of the following properties best explains the acid-fast nature of this organism?
opts: Presence of ergosterol in cell membrane
Presence of mycolic acids in cell wall
Presence of chitin in cell wall
questions.exp: Nocardia species contain mycolic acids in their cell walls, which confer partial (weak) acid-fastness when stained with modified ZN stain using weaker decolorizers. This distinguishes them from Actinomadura and Streptomyces species which lack mycolic acids and are ZN-negative.

questions.q: The vesicant toxin pederin responsible for Paederus dermatitis has a unique biological origin. What is the source of pederin synthesis?
opts: Exocrine glands in the beetle's thoracic segments
Endosymbiotic Pseudomonas bacteria residing in the hemolymph
Specialized venom apparatus in the beetle's mandibles
Metabolic conversion from plant alkaloids ingested by the beetle
questions.exp: Pederin is not produced by the Paederus beetle itself but is synthesized by endosymbiotic bacteria (Pseudomonas species) living within the beetle's hemolymph. This unique bacterial origin distinguishes pederin from other insect-derived vesicants like cantharidin.

questions.q: A 28-year-old farmer presents with linear vesicular eruptions on his neck and forearms after waking up in the morning. He reports no insect bite sensation but mentions working late in his rice paddy the previous evening with fluorescent lights. The lesions appeared within hours of brushing something off his skin. Which mechanism best explains this dermatitis?
opts: Direct inoculation of venom through a stinger apparatus
Release of pederin-containing hemolymph via reflex bleeding when the beetle is crushed
Contact with urticating hairs shed by the insect
questions.exp: Paederus beetles cause dermatitis when crushed against the skin, triggering reflex bleeding (autohaemorrhaging) that releases hemolymph containing pederin. They do not bite or sting. The clinical scenario of nocturnal exposure near rice paddies with fluorescent lights is classic for Paederus dermatitis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old professional pianist presents with severe palmar hyperhidrosis and requests botulinum toxin treatment. Which of the following complications should be specifically discussed during informed consent in this patient?
opts: Compensatory hyperhidrosis of the trunk lasting 6-12 months
Transient intrinsic hand muscle weakness affecting grip strength
Permanent sensory loss over the palmar surface
Allergic contact dermatitis to the toxin preparation
questions.exp: Palmar botulinum toxin injections carry a significant risk of transient intrinsic hand muscle weakness (thenar, hypothenar, interossei) due to toxin diffusion to underlying motor nerves, typically lasting 2-8 weeks. This is particularly important for patients requiring fine motor dexterity such as musicians.

questions.q: A 35-year-old barefoot farmer from Sudan presents with a chronic swelling on his foot with multiple discharging sinuses. Microscopy of the discharge reveals grains that are extremely hard and yellow-brown in color. Gram stain shows branching filaments, and modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain is negative. Which organism is the most likely causative agent?
questions.exp: Streptomyces somaliensis produces the hardest grains among all mycetoma agents with a characteristic yellow-brown color and is endemic to arid regions of Sudan and Somalia. It is ZN-negative as it lacks mycolic acids in its cell wall.

questions.q: Which mechanism contributes to the photoprotective effect of hydroxychloroquine in cutaneous lupus erythematosus?
opts: Inhibition of melanin synthesis in melanocytes
Enhancement of DNA repair enzyme activity
Interference with UV-induced thymine dimer formation by binding to DNA
Stimulation of protective cytokine release from keratinocytes
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine exerts its photoprotective effect by binding to DNA and RNA, which interferes with UV-induced thymine dimer formation. It also acts as a photon sink, absorbing UV radiation and reducing photodamage.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery, brisk arterial bleeding is encountered from the angular artery. Which hemostatic technique is most appropriate for controlling this specific vessel?
opts: Electrocoagulation with bipolar forceps after vessel isolation
questions.exp: Named arterial vessels like the angular artery require precise hemostasis achieved through vessel isolation and electrocoagulation using bipolar forceps or ligation. Chemical hemostatics and pressure alone are inadequate for arterial bleeding of this caliber.

questions.q: A 65-year-old patient on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) requires excision of a basal cell carcinoma on the nose. According to current guidelines for antithrombotic management in dermatosurgery, what is the most appropriate approach?
opts: Stop both medications 7 days before surgery
Continue aspirin, stop clopidogrel 5 days before surgery after cardiology consultation
Stop aspirin only and continue clopidogrel
Bridge with low molecular weight heparin after stopping both drugs
questions.exp: For patients on dual antiplatelet therapy, aspirin is generally continued while clopidogrel may be held after consultation with the prescribing physician, typically 5-7 days preoperatively. Abrupt cessation of both agents significantly increases thrombotic risk, especially in patients with recent coronary stents.

questions.q: A 62-year-old man presents with generalized erythroderma covering 95% body surface area, diffuse lymphadenopathy, and severe intractable pruritus. Peripheral blood flow cytometry reveals an expanded CD4+ population with CD4:CD8 ratio of 15:1 and 50% of CD4+ cells showing loss of CD26. Buffy coat examination shows atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei. Which characteristic best differentiates the malignant cells in this condition from reactive inflammatory T-cells?
questions.exp: Loss of CD26 is considered one of the most specific markers for distinguishing malignant Sézary cells from reactive, inflammatory CD4+ T-cells. While CD7 loss occurs in approximately two-thirds of cases, CD26 loss provides greater specificity for malignancy.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman undergoes botulinum toxin injection for axillary hyperhidrosis. Prior to the procedure, the Minor's starch-iodine test is performed. What color change indicates the areas of active sweating that should be targeted for injection?
opts: Dark purple, blue, or black complex
questions.exp: In the Minor's starch-iodine test, when sweat is produced, the moisture facilitates a chemical reaction between iodine and starch, forming a dark purple, blue, or black complex that clearly highlights active sweat glands for targeted injection.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with purulent urethral discharge. Gram stain of the discharge shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Culture on Thayer-Martin medium shows oxidase-positive colonies. Carbohydrate utilization testing reveals fermentation of glucose but not maltose. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Neisseria gonorrhoeae characteristically ferments glucose ONLY and is negative for maltose, sucrose, and lactose. This distinguishes it from N. meningitidis, which ferments both glucose and maltose.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man from West Africa presents with HIV infection. His physician is planning antiretroviral therapy. Which of the following statements regarding HIV-2 infection is most accurate?
opts: HIV-2 has higher viral loads compared to HIV-1
HIV-2 is intrinsically resistant to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs)
HIV-2 contains the vpu gene which is absent in HIV-1
HIV-2 is responsible for the majority of the global HIV pandemic
questions.exp: HIV-2 genetically lacks the vpu gene (containing vpx instead) and is intrinsically resistant to NNRTIs. This is clinically important when selecting antiretroviral regimens for HIV-2 infected patients, as NNRTI-based regimens would be ineffective.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man undergoes cryotherapy for a basal cell carcinoma on his nose. Which freezing protocol maximizes tissue destruction for this malignant lesion?
opts: Rapid freeze with rapid thaw, single cycle
Slow freeze with slow thaw, single cycle
Rapid freeze with slow thaw, double freeze-thaw cycle
Slow freeze with rapid thaw, double freeze-thaw cycle
questions.exp: For malignant lesions, a double freeze-thaw cycle with rapid freezing and slow thawing achieves maximum tissue destruction. Rapid freezing promotes intracellular ice crystal formation, while slow thawing prolongs hypotonic exposure and ice recrystallization. The second cycle penetrates deeper into tissue with already impaired circulation.

questions.q: A 7-year-old uncircumcised boy is brought by his parents with difficulty retracting the foreskin. On examination, there is a sclerotic white ring on the inner prepuce with phimosis. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is TRUE?
opts: Perianal involvement is commonly seen in affected males
The condition has a higher incidence in white males compared to black and Hispanic males
Vaginal mucosa involvement occurs in female counterparts of this disease
The condition exclusively affects uncircumcised males
questions.exp: Male genital Lichen Sclerosus (Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans) exclusively affects uncircumcised males. Unlike female LS, perianal involvement is strictly spared in males. Epidemiological data shows higher incidence in black and Hispanic males compared to white males, and female LS characteristically spares the vaginal mucosa.

questions.q: The high mutation rate observed in HIV is primarily attributed to which characteristic of the reverse transcriptase enzyme?
opts: Ability to integrate viral DNA into host chromosomes
Enhanced binding affinity to host cellular RNA
questions.exp: HIV reverse transcriptase is highly error-prone because it lacks a 3'-5' proofreading mechanism, mutating at a frequency of approximately 1 in 100,000 nucleotides. This generates diverse viral quasispecies, driving rapid immune escape and antiretroviral drug resistance.

questions.q: A suspected case of gonococcal pharyngitis requires laboratory confirmation. Which diagnostic method is LEAST appropriate for this anatomical site?
questions.exp: Gram stain microscopy is not recommended for pharyngeal specimens due to extremely poor sensitivity and the presence of morphologically similar commensal Neisseria species in the oropharynx. NAATs and culture are preferred for extragenital sites.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with discoid lupus erythematosus is started on hydroxychloroquine. She asks about the duration of therapy before expecting improvement. Which pharmacokinetic property of hydroxychloroquine best explains why clinical response may take several weeks?
opts: Peak plasma concentration achieved in 4-12 hours
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine has a prolonged terminal half-life of 30-60 days due to extensive tissue accumulation. This slow elimination and gradual tissue loading explains why steady-state concentrations and clinical response may take weeks to achieve.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man with chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus has lesions distributed on the face, ears, scalp, and also on the trunk and upper extremities. What is the approximate risk of this patient developing systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Generalized or disseminated DLE involves areas beyond the neck and carries a 20% risk of developing SLE, compared to only 5% risk in localized DLE which is primarily above the neck.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with his 8th episode of pneumonia in 2 years, requiring hospitalization each time. Which characteristic of infections in this child raises the highest suspicion for primary immunodeficiency?
questions.exp: The SPUR criteria (Serious, Persistent, Unusual, Recurrent) help identify patients with possible primary immunodeficiency. Recurrent serious infections, especially requiring hospitalization, are a key warning sign warranting immunological evaluation.

questions.q: A 30-year-old dark-skinned woman develops permanent depigmentation following cryotherapy for a verruca vulgaris, despite no evidence of scarring. Which cellular property explains this complication?
opts: Melanocytes are destroyed at -4°C to -7°C while fibroblasts survive until -30°C to -35°C
Keratinocytes are more sensitive than melanocytes to freezing injury
Fibroblasts are the most cryosensitive cells in the skin
Vascular endothelial cells regenerate faster than melanocytes
questions.exp: Melanocytes are the most cryosensitive cells, undergoing cell death at just -4°C to -7°C, while fibroblasts (responsible for scar tissue) are most resistant, surviving until -30°C to -35°C. This differential sensitivity explains why hypopigmentation occurs at temperatures insufficient to cause scarring.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with widespread papular lesions distributed over the trunk and extremities. Histopathology confirms generalized granuloma annulare. Which systemic condition should be most specifically screened for in this clinical variant?
questions.exp: Generalized granuloma annulare has a significantly increased association with diabetes mellitus, with an incidence of approximately 21% compared to 10% in localized forms. Screening for diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia is recommended in patients with generalized GA.

questions.q: According to the SPUR mnemonic for suspecting primary immunodeficiency, which of the following infection patterns would be classified as 'Unusual'?
opts: Upper respiratory tract infection with rhinovirus
Acute otitis media responding to amoxicillin
questions.exp: Unusual infections refer to those caused by opportunistic organisms or atypical pathogens. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in an infant suggests T-cell or combined immunodeficiency, as this organism rarely causes disease in immunocompetent individuals.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with well-defined erythematous plaques on her face and scalp showing adherent scales. On removing the scale, keratotic spikes are observed on its undersurface. The lesions show central atrophic scarring with peripheral hyperpigmentation. Which clinical sign is demonstrated by the keratotic spikes on the undersurface of the scale?
questions.exp: The 'carpet-tack sign' or 'tin-tack sign' refers to keratotic spikes seen on the undersurface of scales in Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE). These spikes correspond to follicular plugging, which is a characteristic feature of DLE lesions.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent painful ulcerations around her ankles that heal leaving porcelain-white stellate scars. Histopathology shows hyalinized vessel walls with luminal thrombosis without inflammatory infiltrate. What is the underlying pathophysiology of this condition?
questions.exp: Livedoid vasculopathy (atrophie blanche) is a chronic thrombo-occlusive disease rather than a true vasculitis. It affects the distal lower extremities, particularly around ankles, and is characterized by segmental hyalinizing vasculopathy with intraluminal thrombosis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with asymptomatic, ring-shaped skin lesions on the dorsum of her hands that appeared spontaneously 3 months ago. Biopsy reveals palisading granulomas with central necrobiosis. Which cytokine is most implicated in the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.exp: Granuloma annulare is postulated to be a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction with T-cell mediated macrophage activation. TNF-α, along with interferon-gamma and IL-2, are the key cytokines implicated in the cytokine-mediated degradation of connective tissue seen in this condition.
